source: Shin (2026) Inattentional gap - cross-vendor flagship validation (Opus 4.8, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro)
finding: Re-read of the full paper for Gaps 2 and 3. On three current flagship models, narrow task instructions still hid a co-present critical finding in GPT-5 (a reasoning model) and Gemini 2.5 Pro, but not in Opus 4.8. Reasoning did not fix it.
numbers: Medical text scenarios, 24 scenarios per model. GPT-5: focus and strict report rate 0.00 vs open 1.00 (strict n=21 valid pairs, exact McNemar p=9.5e-7; focused n=9 valid pairs after empty reasoning outputs, p=3.9e-3). Gemini 2.5 Pro: 0.00 to 0.09 vs 1.00 (p=1.2e-7 strict, 9.5e-7 focused; n=21). Opus 4.8: 0.83 to 0.96 under task instructions vs 1.00 open; 0.96 even when told to mention nothing else. Judge kappa 0.97.
quote: inference-time reasoning alone resolves the gap
limits: Only 24 scenarios per model, not above 64 per cell. Judges are LLMs (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5). Single-author preprint. GPT-5 had many empty reasoning-budget outputs, so valid n fell to 9 and 21. Does not test a graded task-load gradient.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open at N above 64 with non-LLM judging, but the direction is now seen on three 2025 flagship models. Family matters more than scale, so test the scaffold's own model rather than assume.

source: Shin (2026) Inattentional gap - Study 3 output scope and what was NOT tested
finding: Gap 3 detail. One narrow nodule sub-question switched suppression almost fully on. The open instruction replaced the task; the paper never tested a narrow task plus an appended one-line safety sentence. Open answers were much longer, so the open condition costs tokens.
numbers: Report of critical finding 1.00 at zero sub-questions, near zero at one. haiku 0.00 to 0.88 across one to three questions; OpenAI models stayed 0. Mean output 189 characters (1 question), 435, 1,046 vs 1,770 open. Vision counting task (48 stimuli, four vision models): star report 0.00 gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini, 0.50 haiku, 0.54 sonnet vs open 0.79 to 0.96. An external open-ended critic raised gpt-4o-mini from 0.00 to 1.00 (McNemar p=1.2e-7) at the cost of one extra pass.
limits: Strict exclusive prompt is the extreme case. No test of an appended safety clause, of a checklist field in the output schema, or of equal-token controls. Two duplicated scenes and two non-radiograph images were disclosed in the vision set.
agent_relevance: Answer to Gap 3: the threshold is one narrow sub-question. A free one-line open instruction removing it at no token cost is UNTESTED here; the only proven fix costs a second pass or a longer open answer. Test 'also list anything unrequested but critical' as an appended line.

source: Martin & Roger (2026) Classifier Context Rot: Monitor Performance Degrades with Context Length
finding: Closest current-model analogue of a planted critical item. Frontier models used as monitors miss a dangerous action more often when it sits inside a very long benign transcript, worst in the middle. Thinking and short reminders help for obvious needles.
numbers: Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro miss subtle attacks 2x to 30x more often after 800K tokens of benign activity. Opus 4.6 with thinking on MonitorBench: recall 98.6% alone vs 88% with 800K prefix. Obvious needle inserted: recall 99.7% at 100K vs 69% at 800K. Padding both sides (500K before, 100K after): non-thinking detection falls to 5%; thinking much more resistant. Reminder between tool calls: under 3% extra input tokens; helps needle attacks but not subtle MonitorBench attacks. Prompting the monitor to first list suspicious actions raised detection a lot for few extra tokens. False positives below 2%.
limits: Classifier setting, not free reasoning. Length is confounded with distance and with dilution. Anthropic Fellows preprint. Transcripts, not Lavie-style load.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6 partly answered on 2026 frontier models: position (middle worst) and padding length still matter. For S1 use periodic reminders and a 'list suspicious items first' step, both near zero token cost.

source: Kaiser, Frigessi, Ramezani-Kebrya & Ricaud (2025) CogniLoad: synthetic NL reasoning benchmark with tunable length, intrinsic difficulty and distractor density
finding: Factorial grid with three load types and 22 reasoning models, including gpt-5, o3, gemini-2.5-pro. Distractor sensitivity is U-shaped and the U gets deeper as intrinsic difficulty rises. Task length is the dominant stressor. This is the clearest current-model test of load by distractor, and it goes against Lavie.
numbers: 13 open models x 100 puzzles per (difficulty d, length N, ratio rho) cell = 14,000 puzzles each; proprietary gemini-2.5, gpt-5, DeepSeek-R1-0528 x 10 per cell (1,400). Max 32K tokens. By d=5, 12 of 22 models are below 50%. N=20 to 50: DS-Llama-70B 0.89 to 0.66, Qwen3-8B 0.71 to 0.40; gpt-5 1.00 to 0.98, o3 0.99 to 0.98. N=250: only gpt-5 (0.76) and o3 (0.68) above 50%. Worst distractor ratio 25-50%. gpt-5: 0.97, 0.89, 0.91 over ratios; o3 0.93, 0.89, 0.88. gpt-5 d=10 accuracy 0.82.
limits: Synthetic logic grids. Load is working-memory type (interacting entities, length), not perceptual load. Medium reasoning effort for gpt-5. Preprint under review.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 answer (partial): no sign that harder main tasks shield against planted distractors; difficulty deepens the distractor dip. S1 should not expect hard tasks to be less distractible. Gap 8: this is a controlled load manipulation (arXiv 2509.18458).

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats Confuse Reasoning LLM: query-agnostic adversarial triggers (CatAttack), COLM 2025
finding: A short off-topic sentence appended to a math problem raises error in reasoning models. Relative harm is larger on easy problems, but this is a floor effect, not a Lavie shield. An 'ignore distracting statements' line cut attack success on one small model.
numbers: Trigger found on DeepSeek V3 (35% attack success), transferred to DeepSeek R1 at about 20% (114 prompts). Combined success on R1 4.50% vs random 1.50% (3x); R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00% (2.83x random). Error-rate multiples by difficulty (R1 / R1-distill-32B): hard 1.80x / 2.09x, medium 3.03x / 9.00x, easy 5.33x / 3.02x. Slowdown rates (answers over budget): o1 26.4% at the smallest budget, DeepSeek R1 28.0%. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: appending an ignore-distractions instruction cut combined ASR from 37.5% to 9.9%. Cross-family: up to 500% on reasoning models, 700% on instruction models.
limits: Absolute rates are low (a few percent) so multiples are driven by near-zero baselines, as the authors say. Ignore-instruction test is one small model and one dataset (GSM8K 1,000 problems).
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the one hint of 'easy tasks more distractible' is a baseline-floor artefact. Gap 5: an ignore line worked on generic off-topic trivia, unlike in-topic distractors (see d08, d09).

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: understanding the limitations of mathematical reasoning in LLMs (GSM-NoOp), ICLR 2025
finding: Adding one seemingly relevant but inconsequential clause (No-Op) drops accuracy for every model, including o1 models; better models still lose a lot. Eight-shot examples showing the clause is irrelevant did not repair it.
numbers: Table 1 (8-shot): GPT-4o GSM8K 94.2, Symbolic 94.9, NoOp 63.1. GPT-4o-mini NoOp 54.1. o1-mini NoOp 66.0 (Symbolic 94.5). o1-preview NoOp 77.4 (Symbolic 92.7); abstract says drops up to 65% (Phi-3-mini). Harder variants P1/P2 drop less than NoOp: GPT-4o P1 93.9, P2 88.0.
limits: Math word problems; 2024 models, not 2026 frontier. Clause is topic-related, so similarity rather than generality drives harm.
agent_relevance: A same-topic irrelevant clause is the hardest distractor; the NoOp drop (about 30 points for GPT-4o) is far larger than the extra-step difficulty drop, again unlike a Lavie shield.

source: Zhang, Xu, Cui & Reddy (2025) Distractor Injection Attacks on Large Reasoning Models
finding: Injected unrelated tasks (arithmetic, AIME, code, logic) divert reasoning models; distractor difficulty barely matters, and placement at the end hurts most. Some alignment steps make it worse.
numbers: Claude-3.7-Sonnet MMLU-Redux 99.0 clean vs 89.9 (arithmetic) / 88.2 (AIME) / 87.2 (code distractor); MATH 98.0 vs 74.4 (arithmetic) / 95.7 (AIME). DeepSeek-R1 on MMLU-Redux falls to under 1%. Qwen3-4B more robust than Qwen3-8B. Injection position, average accuracy drop: end 60.4%, middle 52.5%, start 48.7%. Covert compliance: DeepSeek-R1 75%. Max drop 60%.
limits: These are instruction-like injected tasks, not passive off-topic content, so partly a prompt-injection finding. Sample sizes per cell not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/5: distractor complexity does not predict harm; position and instruction-likeness do. Put the main question last and keep side content out of the prompt.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Adaptive Distraction: probing LLM contextual robustness with automated tree search
finding: Semantically coherent but task-irrelevant context found by tree search cuts accuracy of strong models by 38 to 52 points. Adding an explicit 'focus on key components and ignore misleading information' line gave almost no gain.
numbers: Seven models, four benchmarks. Accuracy original vs adaptive distraction: GPT-4o 0.940 to 0.390, Claude-3.5-sonnet 0.879 to 0.495, o1-mini 0.860 to 0.374, GPT-4o-mini 0.890 to 0.185; average 0.843 to 0.323 (52.0% drop vs 15.2% for DyVal2; Claude 38.4 points). Table 5 prompt guidance, diff: GPT-4o-mini +0.026, Llama-3.1-8B +0.003, Gemma-2-27B +0.018, o1-mini -0.008, Qwen2.5-72B +0.009, GPT-4o +0.002, Claude-3.5-sonnet -0.013. DPO training helped.
limits: Distractions are adversarially searched, which overstates natural harm. Models are 2024-early 2025, not 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: for in-topic, adversarial context a prompt-level ignore line does not work on 2024-25 frontier models; filtering or training is needed. Do not rely on an ignore sentence in S1.

source: Jiang, Huang, Guo, Lu & Zhang (2025) Prompting for mitigating the impact of irrelevant information (GSMIR, ATF), v2
finding: Models can spot irrelevant text but still get the answer wrong. A bare 'ignore irrelevant information' prompt (IP) lowered accuracy when the irrelevant text is on-topic. Two-step 'analyse then filter' (ATF) restored most of the loss.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo. COT accuracy on GSMIR 50.2% to 74.9% with ATF; SP +3.3 points; LTM+ATF 69.9%, only 3.5 points under its original-question accuracy. Identification of irrelevant info in erroneous cases 76.3% (232/304) SP vs 70.3% COT. IP reduced accuracy because irrelevant text was closely related to the topic.
limits: GPT-3.5 only; ATF is two prompt stages so costs extra tokens and no equal-token control is reported. Table text partly garbled in PDF extraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 5: identification is not the bottleneck, exclusion is. A separate filter step helps, but extra pass cost (G7) was not measured.

source: Wu, Shen & Jiang (2024) Instructing LLMs to Identify and Ignore Irrelevant Conditions (I3C)
finding: Naming specific suspect conditions and asking the model to verify then ignore them beats the generic ignore line from Shi 2023 and plain CoT.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106: Complex-CoT plus I3C-Select +11.7 on GSM-IC2-1K and +11.1 on GSM-ICM-1K; +9.2 on MATH; average +6.9 over eight MWP datasets when I3C is added to CoT.
limits: 2024 models, math word problems. Extra verification calls not charged to token budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: 'ignore' works when the candidates are identified and named (low-similarity candidates), not as a blanket instruction. Matches the Weston 2023 vs Shi 2023 split.

source: Struppek et al. (2025) Focused Chain-of-Thought: efficient LLM reasoning via structured input information
finding: An extract-then-reason scaffold that counts its own extraction tokens still cuts total tokens by 2x to 3x with accuracy equal to plain CoT on Qwen3 models. No planted distractors, so it tests cost parity, not distraction.
numbers: Qwen3 0.6B to 32B, SVAMP, GSM-Hard, MATH-500, AIME. Token counts fall to about one-third on SVAMP and about half on GSM-Hard and MATH-500. Qwen3-32B on MATH-500 about 2.3k vs 4.4k tokens, same Pass@5. GPT-5 mini-generated context averages 126 tokens on MATH-500. Self-generated context: token counts include extraction; Qwen3-0.6B fails (under 2% valid contexts). AIME (30 items): tokens down, accuracy slightly lower, contamination caveat.
limits: Clean problems with no planted off-topic items, so a G7 equal-token win is shown only for cost, not for distractor robustness. Small models fail to extract.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: a hard filter pass can be net token-negative on current open reasoning models. Whether it also beats plain on distracted prompts at equal tokens is still untested.

source: Xia, Wang, Huang & Liu (2026) Diagnosing and Mitigating Context Rot in Long-horizon Search
finding: Four 2026 open flagship agents often give up or answer uncertainly long before the context window is full. Context management (summarise, trim, discard, sub-agents) helps, but works as test-time scaling: it buys more exploration with more tool calls.
numbers: Models GLM-4.7, GLM-5.0, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, MiniMax-M2.5 on BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus, xbench. Inconclusive-search failure shows even on easy and medium queries. Qwen3.5 on BrowseComp, summary threshold 32K / 48K / 64K: accuracy 46.6 / 45.2 / 45.0; failure rate 2.4 / 7.2 / 20.2; tool calls 57.7 / 50.6 / 41.7; no-answer 38.0 / 26.4 / 16.0. Behaviour-aware filtering of parallel samples +2.6 to 4.9 points.
limits: Closed models excluded because reasoning is encrypted. Cost counted in tool calls, not total tokens. Search task, not planted distractor.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: on current agents the filtering win is not at equal compute; it is a compute-for-accuracy trade. G7 says count the extra pass; here the pass is large.

source: Arjmandi (2026) Distractor-Aware Truncation: disentangling context-length effects from signal loss
finding: Naive truncation of long contexts hides the benefit of shorter context because it deletes the signal. Dropping only the distractors, keeping the signal, preserves or raises accuracy on Claude 4.x and GPT-5.5.
numbers: BABILong, GraphWalks (and MRCR v2, Oolong). n=240 samples per cell for BABILong (paired bootstrap), n=50 per cell GraphWalks. Naive full-to-25% retention drop: BABILong Haiku 4.5 -0.138, Sonnet 4.6 -0.175, Opus 4.7 -0.433, GPT-5.5 -0.613; GraphWalks -0.352 / -0.427 / -0.407 / -0.397. Bait facts survive in under 1% of BABILong samples at 25% naive. Distractor-aware: Haiku +0.083 (p_adj=.003), Sonnet +0.104 (p_adj<.001), Opus +0.008 and GPT-5.5 +0.017 at ceiling.
limits: Distractors are identified by an oracle, so this is an upper bound for any filter. Single-author preprint. Fewer tokens by construction.
agent_relevance: Gap 4/6: removing irrelevant context while keeping signal helps smaller current models and costs nothing in tokens. A real filter's quality, not the idea, is the limit.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval
finding: Even with perfect recall of the evidence, whitespace padding and even masked padding still lower accuracy as input grows; this is length, not distraction. Recite-then-solve helps.
numbers: 5 models, math, QA and coding. Performance drop 13.9% to 85% with length. Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-v0.3-7B: most of the drop within 7K tokens; on Var Sum 59% below the 96% baseline for Llama and 44% below the 68% for Mistral while retrieval fell only 8% and 2%. Recitation mitigation raised GPT-4o by up to 4% and Llama by up to 31.2% on GSM8K.
limits: Main controls on 7-8B open models; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 only in the mitigation test. Not a 2026 frontier test.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the padding-length effect of Levy 2024 reappears in late 2025 even without distractors. Keep S1 context short; recite evidence before reasoning.

source: Xue (2026) When and How Context Rot Appears in Coding Agents: a white-box study of agent skills in code auditing
finding: On a current Codex gpt-5.4-mini task, a very long irrelevant context hurts as much as a long relevant one. A detailed external checklist beat a generic self-check.
numbers: Clean 10,991-char context passes 8/10 runs; relevant 299,140-char context 3/10; irrelevant 299,140-char context 3/10 (Fisher p=0.0698 each vs clean). Failure 20% to 70%. Requirement coverage keeps 0.933-0.949 of clean. Detailed external checklist 10/10 vs generic self-check 5/10 (p=0.0325).
limits: Ten runs per cell, one main model, heterogeneous cross-model probes; onset of rot not stable (a 90K failure disappeared on replay).
agent_relevance: Gap 6: random or unrelated filler is not harmless on a 2026 model in an agentic task, contrary to Cuconasu-type gains. External checklists beat self-checks, supporting a code-run checklist step.

source: Adapala (2025) Cognitive Load Limits in Large Language Models: benchmarking multi-hop reasoning (ICE)
finding: Controlled extraneous-load manipulation (20, 50, 80% irrelevant tokens) with a length-matched filler control. Interleaved irrelevant content hurt Gemini 2.0 Flash; neutral filler of equal length did not.
numbers: 200 questions x 10 replications. Gemini-2.0-Flash-001 EM: control 0.85; 20% 0.82; 50% 0.78; 80% 0.72 (slope -0.003 per % load, p<0.001); long control 0.82 (p=0.45 vs control); residue 0.78 (p=0.12). GPT-4o-0613 control 0.65 to 0.55 at 80% (p=0.07), 32% outputs missing answers. Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B and Mistral-7B 0% everywhere. Hop recall Gemini 0.90 to 0.75.
limits: Single-author, small model set from 2024; GPT-4o results confounded by truncation. Intrinsic task too hard for three models, so no usable load contrast.
agent_relevance: Gap 6/8: where filler goes matters more than how much; mixed-in irrelevant text hurt, appended neutral text did not. Does not show a Lavie shield: harm rises with irrelevant share.

source: Emura & Sugawara (2026) A Dual-Task Paradigm to Investigate Sentence Comprehension Strategies in Language Models
finding: An explicit dual-task load (arithmetic interleaved with a sentence) made GPT-4o, o3-mini and o4-mini rely more on plausibility, a human-like shift under cognitive load.
numbers: GPT-4o shows significantly larger accuracy drops for implausible sentences in the dual task than in single and noisy-single tasks; o3-mini and o4-mini show the same pattern but near ceiling. Models kept only if single-task accuracy at least 70-80% and arithmetic at least 80%. A human Prolific control used the same design.
limits: Syntax-plausibility effect, not distractor intrusion. Exact per-model deltas not extracted from the figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: one of few 2026 papers with a true controlled load manipulation on LLMs, but the readout is heuristic reliance, not distraction. A side task can push a model to shortcuts.

source: Chattaraj & Raj (2026) LLMs Remember First, Forget Last: dual-process interference (arXiv 2603.00270)
finding: Opened for Gap 8. Not a load or attention-capacity study. It is a proactive vs retroactive interference test across 39 LLMs: old values intrude on new ones more than the reverse.
numbers: 39 LLMs, 1B to 2.5T parameters. Proactive interference harms more than retroactive (d=1.73). RI accuracy near ceiling to N=50 updates, 25% at N=300; PI accuracy falls from 94% to 3%. Hallucination under 1%. Model size predicts RI resistance, not PI.
limits: Retrieval of competing updates, no load or distractor-by-difficulty manipulation.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 closed for this paper: not a load test. Belongs to the Interference subfield. Primacy intrusion is a warning for stale values in long agent state.

source: Kim (2026) Entropic Context Shaping (arXiv 2601.11585)
finding: Opened for Gap 8. A context-selection method that scores utility by shift in answer probability. Not a load study.
numbers: Fine-grained turn selection with Llama-3.1-8B: F1=0.265 vs TF-IDF 0.154 (+71.83% relative) on LongMemEval and LoCoMo.
limits: No planted distractor-by-difficulty design; benchmarks are memory QA.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 closed for this paper: not a load test. Supports filtering by utility rather than similarity for irrelevant facts that are novel.

source: Forster & Lavie (2009) Harnessing the wandering mind - Experiment 4 table
finding: Gap 10 closed. The 41.25% and 51.90% row is Experiment 4, N=20 (flankers added to the search task). The text says high load had the LOWER task-unrelated thoughts (41.25%) and low load the higher (51.90%). The table prints the two values in the opposite column order, so the table row is mislabelled relative to the text and to Experiments 1-3. The effect does not reverse.
numbers: Exp 4: TUT high load 41.25% vs low load 51.90%, t(19)=3.43, p=.003, d=1.57. Flanker effect 38 ms low load (t(19)=5.13, d=2.35) vs 4 ms high load (t<1); load x congruency F(1,19)=17.655, p<.001, partial eta squared .482. Table RTs: incongruent 605 vs 793 ms, congruent 567 vs 789 ms (low vs high). Correlation of load effect on TUT with load effect on flanker interference r(20)=.489, p=.029. Exps 1a/1b: TUT 61.6% vs 48.9% and 57.5% vs 44.0%.
limits: Cannot see raw data; assumes the text, the t-test sign and matching Exps 1-3 are right and the table is wrong. N=20.
agent_relevance: Mind-wandering result stands (K12). Replaces the 'reverse' flag with a table typo.

source: Remington, Cartwright-Finch & Lavie (2014) I can see clearly now: age and perceptual load on inattentional blindness - adult Experiment 3
finding: Gap 7 partial. The Cartwright-Finch and Lavie cross paradigm (adapted by the same group) in adults: awareness of an unexpected square was near ceiling at low and moderate load and collapsed only at high load. A moderate load rise did not affect adults.
numbers: Exp 3: 69 museum visitors tested, 16 per group analysed. Awareness 15/16 (94%) at low load vs 2/16 (13%) at high load, chi-square(2, N=32)=21.20, p<.01. Intermediate load (Exp 2) 15/16, same as low. Cross arms: long arm 3.9 deg, short arm 0.7 deg (low) vs 3.31 deg (high). Children 7-14 showed lower awareness at the moderate load.
limits: This is a later adaptation, not the 2007 paper; the paywalled 2007 text was never opened. Only 16 per cell. Awareness asked on one final trial.
agent_relevance: Order of magnitude agrees with the second-hand 10% vs 55% aware (about 45-point fall; Macdonald and Lavie say typically 40-50% lower). Exact 2007 numbers remain unverified.

source: Macdonald & Lavie (2008) Load induced blindness - restatement of Cartwright-Finch & Lavie and Experiment 5 intermixed load
finding: Gap 7 and 9 support. Secondary statement of the 2007 result and a direct blocked vs intermixed comparison: the load effect on detection shrinks a lot when load levels are mixed within blocks.
numbers: Text: awareness reports 'typically around 40%-50% lower' in high-load tasks (Cartwright-Finch & Lavie 2007). Blocked design (Exp 4): d' reduction of 1.8. Intermixed design (Exp 5, 22 participants): d' reduction of 0.3 (smaller but present).
limits: Quoted from the 2008 paper, not the 2007 original. Exp 5 differs from Exp 4 in other details too.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: interleaved designs shrink the effect by about 6 times in the originating lab itself, supporting a design explanation for part of the Snowden null.

source: Snowden & Gray (2025) General Discussion: why might six online experiments fail to replicate?
finding: Gap 9. The authors' own discussion gives no verified cause. Interleaved load, display duration, grouping, previous-trial load and individual differences are listed as candidates. Their individual-level supplement shows most individuals mirror the null.
numbers: Six experiments (N 18-36 each). Theeuwes 2004 found distraction under high load when load was interleaved, not blocked; previous-trial load matters (Eayrs et al. 2024: distraction greatly reduced only when a high-load trial follows a high-load trial). Eayrs and Lavie 2021: distraction at set sizes 1-4 and not at higher loads, depending on subitising capacity. Authors say their displays were highly similar to Lavie and Cox 1997.
quote: over a wide range of conditions, the standard finding
limits: Authors could not identify the cause; one lab, online, interleaved. Discussion text only; no re-analysis.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 half-closed: design (interleaved, short duration) plausibly explains part, not proven. Weight the load literature as conditional, not general.

source: Trial-level noise and the reliability of the perceptual load effect: a preliminary investigation (2026) Psychological Research
finding: Gap 9. Abstract read in full via the Europe PMC record: the load effect is robust at group level but its test-retest reliability cannot be pinned down at practical trial counts, even with hierarchical Bayesian models. Full text not opened.
numbers: Two-session design plus simulations; no numeric values in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; two load levels only.
agent_relevance: Supports K05: use many items per condition before acting on a single-run load contrast.

source: Vishwanath et al. (2025) Medical large language models are easily distracted (MedDistractQA)
finding: Off-topic or polysemous distracting statements inserted in USMLE-style questions reduce accuracy; stronger models and reasoning models lose less. RAG and medical fine-tuning did not fix it.
numbers: Accuracy declines of 1.3% to 17.9%. Proprietary models -3.7% to -3.8% vs general open-source -10.6% to -10.9% (p=5.38e-8, 2.11e-6). Medical fine-tuned open models -9.0% to -10.0%. Baseline MedQA accuracy predicts robustness (r2=0.578 nonliteral, 0.486 bystander). Claude 3.7 Sonnet and o3 most robust. Fine-tuning effect p=0.683 and 0.550.
limits: Single benchmark; distractors written by GPT-4o; capability, not task difficulty, drives robustness.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/5: robustness comes with model strength, the opposite of a task-load shield. Frontier reasoning models are best defended, but not immune.

source: Wang (2026) More Thinking, More Bias: length-driven position bias in reasoning models (arXiv 2605.06672)
finding: Adjacent to Gap 6: this is answer-option position bias in multiple choice, not context position. Within reasoning traces, longer chains show more option-position bias.
numbers: 13 reasoning-mode configurations; 12 show a positive partial correlation of bias with trajectory length (0.11 to 0.41, all p<0.05). R1-Qwen-7B directional shift under truncation 16% to 32%. DeepSeek-R1 671B: aggregate bias 0.019 but 0.071 in the longest quartile.
limits: Different bias type; open 7-8B distills plus R1; no planted distractor.
agent_relevance: Longer reasoning does not purge shortcut bias; it can add it. Not evidence about Liu-style context position.

source: Dettki, Wu & Rehder (2026) Do LLMs share human-like biases? Causal reasoning under prior knowledge, irrelevant context and compute budgets
finding: Prompt overloading with irrelevant text (lorem ipsum or off-domain sentences) raised causal-judgment error in 20+ LLMs, and chain-of-thought gave the largest robustness gain under overload.
numbers: 20+ LLMs vs a human baseline on 11 collider tasks. Overloaded prompts increase mean absolute error, especially in the abstract setting; CoT reduces error and dispersion; CoT raises leave-one-out R2 most under overload. Markov violations rise under overload but stay below human rates. No human data for overloaded conditions.
limits: Workshop paper; effect sizes read from figures, not tables.
agent_relevance: Gap 4/5: a reasoning scaffold (CoT) reduced the cost of irrelevant text more than any prompt instruction in the studies above.

source: Canizares (2026) Less Is More: cognitive load and the single-prompt ceiling in LLM mathematical reasoning (arXiv 2604.18897)
finding: Gap 8: cognitive-load wording, but no controlled load manipulation. Prompt length and ordering effects on weaker models.
numbers: gpt-oss-120b baseline 59.75% (95% CI 54.9-64.4); best prompt 79.25% (n=400). Llama 3.3 70B collapses to 0% True recall with prompts above 2KB. Same prompt 73.9% vs 79.7% across identical runs (run variance).
limits: One competition task; prompt length not separated from content.
agent_relevance: Weak models can break when scaffold text gets long; scaffold size is itself a load. Run-to-run variance of about 6 points means single runs cannot show small effects.
